claim: Chronic pain is a prevalent and debilitating condition whose neural mechanisms are incompletely understood.
source: Chronic pain is a prevalent and debilitating condition whose neural mechanisms are incompletely understood.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of knowledge in the field, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: An imbalance of cerebral excitation and inhibition (E/I), particularly in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), is believed to represent a crucial mechanism in the development and maintenance of chronic pain.
source: An imbalance of cerebral excitation and inhibition (E/I), particularly in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), is believed to represent a crucial mechanism in the development and maintenance of chronic pain.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific consensus and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The aperiodic component of the electroencephalography (EEG) power spectrum has been proposed to represent a non-invasive proxy for E/I.
source: Recently, the aperiodic component of the electroencephalography (EEG) power spectrum has been proposed to represent a non-invasive proxy for E/I.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in the field.

claim: The study assessed the aperiodic component in the mPFC of resting-state EEG recordings in 149 people with chronic pain and 115 healthy participants.
source: We, therefore, assessed the aperiodic component in the mPFC of resting-state EEG recordings in 149 people with chronic pain and 115 healthy participants.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size of the study.

claim: There is robust evidence against differences in the aperiodic component in the mPFC between people with chronic pain and healthy participants.
source: We found robust evidence against differences in the aperiodic component in the mPFC between people with chronic pain and healthy participants, and no correlation between the aperiodic component and pain intensity.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by statistical analysis of the collected data.

claim: There is no correlation between the aperiodic component and pain intensity.
source: We found robust evidence against differences in the aperiodic component in the mPFC between people with chronic pain and healthy participants, and no correlation between the aperiodic component and pain intensity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by statistical analysis of the collected data.

claim: The findings were consistent across different subtypes of chronic pain.
source: These findings were consistent across different subtypes of chronic pain and were similarly found in a whole-brain analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the subgroup analyses presented in the results section.

claim: The findings were similarly found in a whole-brain analysis.
source: These findings were consistent across different subtypes of chronic pain and were similarly found in a whole-brain analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the whole-brain analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The robustness of the findings was supported by preregistration and multiverse analyses across many different methodological choices.
source: Their robustness was supported by preregistration and multiverse analyses across many different methodological choices.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used to validate the findings.

claim: The EEG aperiodic component does not differentiate between people with chronic pain and healthy individuals.
source: Together, our results suggest that the EEG aperiodic component does not differentiate between people with chronic pain and healthy individuals.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: Chronic pain is a highly prevalent disease.
source: Chronic pain is a highly prevalent disease (Kennedy et al., 2014) that severely decreases the quality of life of those who live with it, and imposes a substantial burden on society and healthcare systems (Rice et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kennedy et al., 2014.

claim: Chronic pain severely decreases the quality of life of those who live with it.
source: Chronic pain is a highly prevalent disease (Kennedy et al., 2014) that severely decreases the quality of life of those who live with it, and imposes a substantial burden on society and healthcare systems (Rice et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kennedy et al., 2014 and Rice et al., 2016.

claim: Chronic pain imposes a substantial burden on society and healthcare systems.
source: Chronic pain is a highly prevalent disease (Kennedy et al., 2014) that severely decreases the quality of life of those who live with it, and imposes a substantial burden on society and healthcare systems (Rice et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rice et al., 2016.

claim: The neural mechanisms of chronic pain are incompletely understood, and effective therapies are lacking.
source: The neural mechanisms of chronic pain are incompletely understood, and effective therapies are lacking (Cohen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cohen et al., 2021.

claim: Human and animal studies have revealed structural and functional changes in an extended network of brain areas in chronic pain, including the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC).

claim: Cellular and microcircuit studies in rodent models of chronic pain have indicated imbalances between neural excitation and inhibition in the brain network involved in chronic pain.
source: Cellular and microcircuit studies in rodent models of chronic pain have indicated imbalances between neural excitation and inhibition in this network (Bliss et al., 2016; Kummer et al., 2020; Shiers and Price, 2020; Tan and Kuner, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bliss et al., 2016; Kummer et al., 2020; Shiers and Price, 2020; Tan and Kuner, 2021.

claim: PET and MRS studies in humans have suggested alterations in the excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance in experimental and chronic pain.
source: Correspondingly, positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) studies in humans have suggested alterations in the excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance in experimental and chronic pain (Pasanta et al., 2023; Peek et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pasanta et al., 2023; Peek et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2017.

claim: Changes in E/I likely relate to central sensitization.
source: Furthermore, changes in E/I likely relate to central sensitization (Woolf, 2011), which has been observed in many chronic pain states, including nociplastic pain conditions (Kaplan et al., 2024).

claim: Central sensitization has been observed in many chronic pain states, including nociplastic pain conditions.

claim: Recent studies have highlighted the physiological significance of the power spectrum's aperiodic (1/fχ) component.

claim: The slope of the aperiodic component, given by the aperiodic exponent (χ), has been linked to the E/I balance.

claim: Dataset 3 has not been previously analyzed or published and includes 27 healthy participants.
source: Dataset 3 has not been previously analyzed or published and includes 27 healthy participants.

claim: The gender ratio of both groups was similar (people with chronic pain: 98 females and 53 males, healthy: 74 females and 41 males).
source: The gender ratio of both groups was similar (people with chronic pain: 98 females and 53 males, healthy: 74 females and 41 males).

claim: The total sample included participants of a wide age range (people with chronic pain: 86–18, healthy: 79–18).
source: The total sample included participants of a wide age range (people with chronic pain: 86–18, healthy: 79–18) but mostly white men and women who were currently pursuing or previously acquired higher education.

claim: EEG data was recorded with 64 passive electrodes in the standard 10/20 positions.
source: EEG data was recorded with 64 pasive electrodes in the standard 10/20 positions (Easycap, Hersching, Germany) and a BrainAmp MR plus amplifier (Brain Products GmbH, Gilching, Germany).
evidence: This describes the data acquisition methods.

claim: For most participants, two blocks of 5 min each were recorded, one with eyes closed and one with eyes open.
source: For most participants, two blocks of 5 min each were recorded, one with eyes closed and one with eyes open.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition methods.

claim: This study only analyzed the eyes closed condition, available for all participants.
source: This study only analyzed the eyes closed condition, available for all participants.
evidence: This describes the data used in the study.

source: One participant in Dataset 2 was excluded because they had already been included in Dataset 1.

source: Another participant of Dataset 2 was excluded due to technical problems during the recording.

claim: The final sample size was 149 people with chronic pain and 115 healthy participants.
source: Therefore, the final sample size was 149 people with chronic pain and 115 healthy participants.

claim: EEG data was automatically preprocessed in MATLAB with the default settings of the DISCOVER-EEG pipeline version 1.0.0.
source: EEG data was automatically preprocessed in MATLAB (Mathworks, Natick, MA), with the default settings of the DISCOVER-EEG pipeline version 1.0.0. (Gil Ávila et al., 2023; Pernet et al., 2020) using the EEGLAB Toolbox (Delorme and Makeig, 2004).
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing methods, supported by citations.

claim: No recording was discarded based on preprocessing outcomes.
source: No recording was discarded based on preprocessing outcomes.
evidence: This describes the data quality control procedures.

claim: For subgroup analyses, two subgroups were defined based on the clinical diagnosis: people with Chronic Back Pain (CBP, N=80) and people with Chronic Widespread Pain (CWP, N=33).
source: For subgroup analyses (Research Question 2), we defined two subgroups based on the clinical diagnosis: people with Chronic Back Pain (CBP, N=80) and people with Chronic Widespread Pain (CWP, N=33).
evidence: This describes the subgroup analysis approach.

claim: A source reconstruction of the preprocessed, segmented, and band-passed filtered signals was performed to spatially localize brain activity.
source: To spatially localize brain activity, we performed a source reconstruction of the preprocessed, segmented, and band-passed filtered signals.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods.

claim: The data was projected to source space using an array-gain Linear Constrained Minimum Variance (LCMV) beamformer.
source: We projected the data to source space using an array-gain Linear Constrained Minimum Variance (LCMV) beamformer.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods.

claim: The centroid regions of the 100-parcel version of the Schaefer atlas with 17 networks was used as a source model.
source: As a source model, we used the centroid regions of the 100-parcel version of the Schaefer atlas with 17 networks (Schaefer et al., 2018; Yeo et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods, supported by citations to Schaefer et al., 2018 and Yeo et al., 2011.

claim: The primary region of interest, the medial prefrontal cortex, was defined as all the parcels from the Schaefer atlas labeled medial prefrontal cortex ('PFCm'), medial posterior prefrontal cortex ('PFCmp'), and anterior cingulate cortex ('Cinga').
source: We defined our primary region of interest, the medial prefrontal cortex, as all the parcels from the above-mentioned version of the Schaefer atlas labeled medial prefrontal cortex ('PFCm'), medial posterior prefrontal cortex ('PFCmp'), and anterior cingulate cortex ('Cinga').
evidence: This describes the region of interest definition.

claim: Four parcels comprised the mPFC by this definition.
source: Four parcels comprised the mPFC by this definition (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the region of interest definition, shown in Figure 1.

claim: Power spectra were parametrized into periodic and aperiodic components with a re-implementation in MATLAB of the 'spectparam' algorithm, formally known as FOOOF.
source: Power spectra were parametrized into periodic and aperiodic components with a re-implementation in MATLAB of the 'spectparam' algorithm, formally known as FOOOF (Donoghue et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods, supported by a citation to Donoghue et al., 2020.

claim: With the pre-registered settings, the power spectra of all participants could be satisfactorily modeled (MAE = 0.03 ± 0.01, R2=0.98 ± 0.01 [mean ± std]).
source: With the pre-registered settings, the power spectra of all participants could be satisfactorily modeled (MAE = 0.03 ± 0.01, R2=0.98 ± 0.01 [mean ± std]).
evidence: This describes the quality of the model fit.

claim: No participant was excluded based on a poor model fit.
source: Thus, no participant was excluded based on a poor model fit.
evidence: This describes the data quality control procedures.

claim: With the pre-defined sample size, an α error probability of 0.05, and a statistical power of 0.95, the study could detect medium effect sizes (Cohen's d=0.44).
source: With our pre-defined sample size, given that the data had already been acquired, an α error probability of 0.05, and a statistical power of 0.95, we could detect medium effect sizes (Cohen's d=0.44).
evidence: This describes the statistical power of the study.

claim: Age was controlled for by using linear regression models to remove the influence of age from aperiodic exponents and pain intensity ratings.
source: To control for age effects, we used linear regression models to remove the influence of age from aperiodic exponents and pain intensity ratings.
evidence: This describes the statistical methods used to control for confounding variables.
